testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: why can't we test an LLM app the same way we test normal software?
testCases.actualOutput:
To understand why we cannot test an LLM application the same way we test normal software, we have to look at how their fundamental natures differ. 

Let's start with the basic intuition. Think of normal software like a standard calculator. If you type in two plus two, it will always, without fail, give you four. It does not matter if you do it once or ten thousand times; the result is completely predictable. Because of this predictability, testing normal software is very straightforward. You can quickly write specific test cases to check if the inputs lead to the expected outputs, and if they do, you know the software is working.

In technical terms, we say that normal software is **deterministic**. This means that if you give the system the exact same input, you are guaranteed to get the exact same output every single time. For example, if you put in the correct email and password, you will always log in, and if you put them in wrong, you won't. 

LLMs and LLM-based applications, however, are entirely different because they are **probabilistic**. When we say a system is probabilistic, it means that if you give it the exact same input again and again, it is possible—and even likely—that you will get different outputs. A simple example of this is when you go to ChatGPT and search for the same prompt multiple times; you will get different responses. 

Because LLM applications are probabilistic, we cannot simply write quick, rigid test cases to evaluate them. Once real users start interacting with your application, you can never truly know what questions they will ask or exactly how the chatbot will respond. This makes evaluating LLM-based applications incredibly tricky. Instead of relying on straightforward software test cases, we have to think deeply about all the different factors that matter and actually create our own custom rubrics to properly evaluate the system's behavior.
testCases.expectedOutput: Normal software is deterministic and rule-based, so the same input always gives the same output and you can assert one exact expected value. LLM applications are probabilistic, so the same input can produce different wordings, and most tasks have many acceptable answers instead of one exact string. That breaks exact-match testing, so LLM evaluation instead judges qualities of the output, usually against a golden dataset and often with an LLM as a judge.
